items.stem: Explain how the findings of Festinger, Riecken and Schachter (1956) provide evidence about how belief is maintained when expectations are disconfirmed.
items.answer: Findings: when the flood did not happen, the most committed members did not abandon their beliefs but began recruiting more actively, consistent with reducing cognitive dissonance. Link: these results are evidence about how belief is maintained when expectations are disconfirmed.

items.stem: Describe the study by Curtiss (1977) and explain what it shows about the critical period hypothesis for language.
items.answer: Curtiss (1977). Aim: to study the language development of a girl who had been severely isolated until age 13. Method: Genie was found in Los Angeles in 1970 after years of isolation and neglect; she was studied over several years with observations, language tests and recordings. Findings: Genie learned many words but never developed normal grammar, consistent with a critical period for language acquisition Link: the critical period hypothesis for language.

items.stem: Using Festinger, Riecken and Schachter (1956) as supporting evidence, explain how belief is maintained when expectations are disconfirmed.
items.answer: Festinger, Riecken and Schachter (1956). Aim: to observe how members of a doomsday group would respond when their prophecy failed. Method: The researchers joined a small group in the USA whose leader predicted a flood on 21 December 1954, posing as believers and recording members' behaviour before and after the date. Findings: when the flood did not happen, the most committed members did not abandon their beliefs but began recruiting more actively, consistent with reducing cognitive dissonance Link: how belief is maintained when expectations are disconfirmed.

items.stem: Using Milgram's obedience study as an example, explain ethical guidelines in research.
items.answer: Participants believed they were giving increasingly strong electric shocks to a learner; many showed extreme stress - sweating, trembling, nervous laughter - yet the experimenter told them "you have no other choice, you must go on". It breached protection from harm, used deception, and the prods undermined the right to withdraw; Milgram defended it with debriefing and a follow-up in which 84% said they were glad to have taken part

items.stem: Using Milgram (1963) as supporting evidence, explain the power of situational factors in obedience.
items.answer: Milgram (1963). Aim: to investigate how far people would obey an authority figure who instructed them to harm another person. Method: 40 male volunteers from New Haven, recruited by newspaper advertisement, acted as "teachers" giving apparent shocks of 15-450 V to a confederate "learner" at Yale University when he made errors; the experimenter used four standard prods. Findings: 65% (26/40) went to the maximum 450 V and all went to at least 300 V; many showed extreme tension Link: the power of situational factors in obedience.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: 65% (26/40) went to the maximum 450 V and all went to at least 300 V; many showed extreme tension); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to the power of situational factors in obedience. items.stem: Using Watson and Rayner (1920) as supporting evidence, explain classical conditioning of emotional responses.

Findings: Albert came to cry at the rat alone and the fear generalised to similar objects (a rabbit, a fur coat) Link: classical conditioning of emotional responses.

items.stem: With reference to Watts, Duncan and Quan (2018), explain how research has investigated the generalisability of findings from narrow samples.
items.answer: Watts, Duncan and Quan (2018). Aim: to test whether the link between early delay of gratification and later achievement replicated in a larger, more diverse sample. Method: Data from about 900 children in the US NICHD Study of Early Child Care were analysed; delay time at 54 months was correlated with achievement at age 15, controlling for family background and early cognitive ability. Findings: the association was about half the size of earlier findings and, once family background and early ability were controlled, it became very small Link: the generalisability of findings from narrow samples.

items.stem: Using Mischel, Ebbesen and Zeiss (1972) as supporting evidence, explain the role of cognitive strategies in self-control.
items.answer: Mischel, Ebbesen and Zeiss (1972). Aim: to investigate how cognitive strategies affect children's ability to delay gratification. Method: Pre-school children at the Stanford University nursery were offered one treat now or two if they waited for the experimenter to return; conditions varied whether the treats were visible and whether children were given distraction instructions. Findings: children waited longer when the rewards were hidden or when they were given distracting thoughts; later follow-ups linked longer waiting to higher adolescent competence Link: the role of cognitive strategies in self-control.

items.stem: A student plans to observe how often classmates check their phones in the library, without telling them. Identify two ethical issues and suggest how each could be addressed.
items.answer: Consent - it may be acceptable as a public-place observation, but participants should be debriefed afterwards or the observation made overt; confidentiality - record no names or identifying details; right to withdraw - offer to destroy data on request.
items.markingKey: Consent - it may be acceptable as a public-place observation, but participants should be debriefed afterwards or the observation made overt; confidentiality - record no names or identifying details; right to withdraw - offer to destroy data on request.

items.stem: Using Open Science Collaboration (2015) as supporting evidence, explain the reliability of published psychological research.
items.answer: Open Science Collaboration (2015). Aim: to estimate how many published psychology findings could be reproduced. Method: 270 researchers attempted to replicate 100 studies from three leading psychology journals (2008), using the original materials where possible and high-powered designs. Findings: 97% of the original studies had significant results but only about 36% of the replications did; effect sizes in replications were about half the size Link: the reliability of published psychological research.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: 97% of the original studies had significant results but only about 36% of the replications did; effect sizes in replications were about half the size); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to the reliability of published psychological research. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: With reference to Becker et al. (2002), explain how research has investigated the role of interviews in explaining cultural change in behaviour.
items.answer: Becker et al. (2002). Aim: to investigate the impact of the introduction of Western television on disordered eating attitudes in Fijian adolescent girls. Method: Ethnic Fijian schoolgirls completed the EAT-26 questionnaire in 1995 (just after TV arrived) and in 1998; in 1998 a subsample of 30 girls also took part in semi-structured interviews. Findings: the percentage scoring high on the EAT-26 rose from 12.7% to 29.2%, and self-induced vomiting to control weight rose from 0% to 11.3%; interviews revealed admiration for TV characters and a link between thinness and success Link: the role of interviews in explaining cultural change in behaviour.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: the percentage scoring high on the EAT-26 rose from 12.7% to 29.2%, and self-induced vomiting to control weight rose from 0% to 11.3%; interviews revealed admiration for TV characters and a link between thinness and success); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to the role of interviews in explaining cultural change in behaviour. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Psychology is in a replication crisis, so its findings cannot be trusted."
items.answer: The replication crisis shows the need for caution and reform, but it does not mean all findings are untrustworthy; well-replicated findings remain credible.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: only about 36% of replications were significant (OSC, 2015); publication bias and p-hacking; small samples. items.stem: With reference to the six concepts of the course, discuss the claim that triangulation makes qualitative findings as trustworthy as experimental findings.
items.answer: Triangulation strengthens credibility but answers different questions from experiments; trustworthiness depends on the aims of the research.

To investigate how far people would obey an authority figure who instructed them to harm another person
To investigate the impact of the introduction of Western television on disordered eating attitudes in Fijian adolescent girls
To investigate whether a fear response could be classically conditioned in a human infant

items.stem: Which research method best describes the study by Mischel, Ebbesen and Zeiss (1972) on delay of gratification in pre-school children?

items.answer: The researcher is the main instrument of data collection and interpretation, so their background and assumptions can shape what is asked and how answers are interpreted; reflexivity makes this influence visible and allows readers to judge credibility.
